text:
The week opened with the news Jordan had been bracing for since August: the reorg landed on 9/1, one day late, and it wasn't a layoff — it was worse in a quieter way. Internal tools is dissolving, and Jordan is being moved to legacy marketing pages under a new manager, Priya, starting the 21st. Marcus delivered it in fifteen minutes and called it "broadening surface area," which Jordan clocked immediately for what it was: the holding pen, the place people get parked before eventual severance. No relief came, just a flat gray feeling. Lena, who starts her own new job Friday, named it outright — "that's the holding pen and you know it" — and told Jordan to hang on.

What's notable is what Jordan did with the spiral that started loading. Instead of the usual full shutdown — blinds down, phone off, sometimes needing Mika to physically show up — Jordan sat on the couch in the dark for twenty minutes, coat still on, then got up and went to Groundwork to work on Coda for two hours. Jordan flagged this carefully, not wanting to overclaim one good night, but noted the pattern explicitly: the middle part, the dark stretch before recovery, got shorter this time, and it happened alone.

Two days later, on 9/3, Coda ran into its first real user outside Jordan: Dev, sideloaded onto their phone, practicing for forty minutes in Jordan's living room. The session surfaced something Jordan hadn't designed for. Jordan's own nine days of free play had only caught surface friction — button size, session length. Dev's eleven marked moments were all failures, things to fix before a gig on the 19th, and Dev treated the app as a bug tracker without hesitation. Jordan realized the whole review screen was built around "highlights" and "best moments" — a trophy case — because Jordan's own use of the app had been about collecting evidence of being okay, not about deliberate practice toward a deadline. The gap became a design insight: don't name the marks at all, let the person decide what they mean. Dev, unprompted, found a years-old crutch in their own playing within ninety seconds of looking at the data, and then drilled their worst-marked moment four times until it wasn't the worst anymore — with Pepper registering her opinion by leaving and returning.

The week closed with Mom's Labor Day visit (9/6). Small, warm details — the folding chair she remembered to bring, the green rug she liked, Dad's old guitar picks handed over unprompted, Pepper sleeping on her lap. But the real event was on the walk at Greenwood Park: Jordan finally told her everything about work, five weeks after deciding to keep her out of it specifically to protect her. Her response wasn't anger, just sadness — "I wish you'd told me in July" — and sharper questions than Jordan had asked himself. Jordan ended the week naming the pattern out loud: this is what he does, with Mika, with Dev, with Mom — blackout first, disclosure late. That habit, and what to do with legacy marketing starting the 21st, are both unresolved heading into next week.
